gbs333-aa6045-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether the habit of theology is really one in number.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e118.summary: Summarizes Ockham's treatment: after rejecting two opinions, he answers first about habits in general, then about theology, then raises four doubts. Acquired habits are distinguished as the acts from which they arise are distinguished; assent to a principle differs from assent to a conclusion, and assents to different propositions differ not only in number but in species, as the propositions do, since non-synonymous mental propositions differ more than synonymous ones, which already differ in number. Hence total sciences like metaphysics or natural philosophy are not numerically one habit but aggregates of specifically distinct habits with some order, and acquired theology likewise is not one habit, unlike infused faith, which is numerically one in a given intellect.
claims: Acquired habits are distinguished according to the acts that generate them.
Assents to non-synonymous propositions differ in species.
Total sciences such as metaphysics are ordered aggregates of specifically distinct habits, not one habit.
Acquired theology is not one habit; infused faith is numerically one in one intellect.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e189.summary: First dictum on habits in general: a habit acquired from acts concerning a principle is distinct from the habit of the conclusion. The habit of the principle is a mediate cause of the habit of the conclusion (it causes assent to the principle, which with a minor premise generates actual knowledge of the conclusion, which generates the habit), and every cause is distinct from its effect. Also, per Posterior Analytics I, the habit of principles is more perfect than that of conclusions.
claims: The habit of a principle is distinct from the habit of its conclusion.
The habit of the principle is a mediate cause of the habit of the conclusion.
Every cause is distinct from its effect.
The habit of principles is more perfect than the habit of conclusions.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e226.summary: Second dictum: distinct conclusions have distinct habits, because they have distinct acts, and habits are always proportioned in identity and diversity to the acts that generate or increase them, since habits incline immediately to acts and only through acts to objects.
claims: Distinct conclusions have distinct habits.
Habits are as identical or diverse as the acts generating them.
Habits incline immediately to acts and only mediately to objects.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e255.summary: Third dictum: sometimes there can be a single habit of conclusion and principles together, since one can assent by a single act to a whole demonstration taken as one hypothetical (conditional) proposition. One adhesive act suffices for any single proposition—categorical, hypothetical, or consequential—because it is one truth; if a single act can assent to a proposition of few terms, so can it to one of many.
claims: A single habit can cover principles and conclusion together.
A whole demonstration can be assented to by one act as a single hypothetical proposition.
One act of assent suffices for any single proposition, however complex.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e288.summary: Fourth dictum: the identity and diversity of habits follows the specific identity and diversity of the acts that generate them, not that of their objects. Ockham also notes (Prologue q. 1 and below q. 9) that 'one science' is sometimes taken for a collection of many habits with a determinate order, owing to conclusions ordered by the unity of their subject or predicate (e.g. diverse attributes demonstrated of one subject, or one attribute of diverse subjects); this is how philosophers commonly speak of the unity of a science.
claims: Habits are individuated by the specific identity of acts, not by objects.
A science is called one as an ordered collection of habits united by subject or predicate.
This is the common philosophical sense of the unity of a science.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e340.summary: Distinguishes two senses of 'theology': (1) the same as infused faith, in which sense it is numerically one habit in one intellect (treated more fully in Book III); (2) including acquired faith, evident adhesive habits of propositions and conclusions, and apprehensive habits of all the complexes and incomplexes treated in acquired theology, in which case, as the acts of believing and assenting differ in species, so do the habits generated from them.
claims: Theology identical with infused faith is numerically one habit.
Theology as including acquired faith, evident habits, and apprehensive habits is a plurality of specifically distinct habits.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e377.summary: First conclusion: taking theology as identical with or including infused faith, it can be called numerically one; this is to be discussed in Book III.
claims: Theology as infused faith is numerically one.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e391.summary: Second conclusion: taking theology as including acquired faith, evident acquired habits of propositions and consequences, and apprehensive acts of complexes and incomplexes, it is not numerically one, because diverse acts have diverse habits and these acts differ in species and number.
claims: Acquired theology is not numerically one habit.
Diverse acts yield diverse habits.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e411.summary: Transitional sentence announcing that Ockham now raises four doubts.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e416.summary: First doubt, how the habits of principle and conclusion compare in perfection: the habit of principles is more perfect because more evident, and the nobility of habits is measured by evidence and the nobility of the object; the conclusion's object is also a partial object of some principle.
claims: The habit of principles is more perfect than the habit of conclusions.
The nobility of a habit depends on its evidence and the nobility of its object.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e438.summary: Second doubt, whether the habit of principles causes the habit of the conclusion: knowledge of principles is the efficient cause not of the conclusion but of knowledge of the conclusion. The premises do not cause the conclusion, since each can be formed without the other; but once premises, conclusion, and knowledge of the premises are given, knowledge of the conclusion follows at once.
claims: Knowledge of principles efficiently causes knowledge of the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
Premises and conclusion can each be formed without the other.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e475.summary: Third doubt, why a habit of principles must be posited at all, since the intellect is already determined to maximally self-evident principles and a determined power needs no determining habit. The solution is deferred to Book III.
claims: The necessity of a habit of self-evident principles is questioned and deferred to Book III.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e491.summary: Fourth doubt, what the single habit covering principles and conclusion is: it is wisdom, which is equivalently understanding and science, the habit of a whole demonstration, as understanding is the habit of the principle and science of the conclusion. Wisdom is taken generally for the habit of a whole demonstration from first principles, found even in the mechanical arts (the wise mason or sculptor, Ethics VI), or specifically for the habit of demonstration of the noblest objects. Its distinctness from understanding and science is proved from Aristotle and by reason: every necessary proposition is a principle or a conclusion, so wisdom must be of both together, i.e., of the whole demonstration. Q. 9 follows.
claims: The single habit of principle and conclusion together is wisdom.
Wisdom is equivalently understanding and science, the habit of a whole demonstration.
Wisdom is taken broadly, even in mechanical arts, or strictly, for demonstration of the noblest objects.
Wisdom differs from understanding and science because it concerns principle and conclusion together.

gbs333-aa6045-d1e566.summary: Transitional rubric introducing the second part of the prologue, on the subject of theology, which begins with the following question.

gbs333-aa6045.summary: Quaestio 8 asks whether the habit of theology is numerically one. Following Ockham, Biel argues that acquired habits are individuated by the acts that generate them, not by their objects. Since assents to principles and to conclusions, and to different non-synonymous propositions, differ in species, total sciences such as metaphysics are ordered aggregates of specifically distinct habits, called 'one' only by the order their conclusions take from a common subject or predicate. Four dicta establish that the habit of a principle differs from that of its conclusion, that distinct conclusions have distinct habits, that a whole demonstration can nonetheless be the object of a single habit through one act of assent to a hypothetical proposition, and that habits follow the specific diversity of acts. Distinguishing theology as infused faith from acquired theology, he concludes that the former is numerically one while the latter is a plurality of habits. Four doubts follow. The habit of principles is more perfect because more evident. Knowledge of principles causes knowledge of the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. The need for a habit of self-evident principles is deferred to Book III. The single habit of a whole demonstration is wisdom, equivalently understanding and science together. A closing rubric opens the second part of the prologue, on theology's subject.
claims: Habits are individuated by the specific diversity of the acts generating them, not by their objects.
Total sciences and acquired theology are ordered aggregates of many specifically distinct habits, not numerically one habit.
Theology taken as infused faith is numerically one habit.
Wisdom is the single habit of a whole demonstration, equivalent to understanding and science together.
